questions.question: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and why do companies use it?
questions.answer: IaC is the practice of managing cloud infrastructure through code files instead of manual console actions. Companies use it because it ensures environment consistency (same code = same result every time), enables fast disaster recovery (re-run the code to rebuild everything), supports reusability across teams and environments, provides a full audit trail through version control, and eliminates human error from repetitive manual configuration.

questions.question: What is the difference between declarative and imperative IaC?
questions.answer: Declarative IaC describes your desired final state — you say what you want (e.g., 'I want an EC2 instance with t3.micro') and the tool figures out how to create it. Imperative IaC specifies exact step-by-step instructions in order. CloudFormation and Terraform are declarative. Ansible playbooks can be imperative when you write ordered tasks. Declarative is preferred because it's simpler and less error-prone.

questions.question: What is the difference between a CloudFormation Template and a Stack?
questions.answer: A Template is the blueprint — a YAML or JSON file that describes what resources you want to create and how they should be configured. A Stack is the actual collection of AWS resources that CloudFormation creates from that template. One template can be used to create multiple stacks (e.g., one for dev, one for production). All resources in a stack are managed together.

questions.question: Which section of a CloudFormation template is mandatory? What are the optional sections?
questions.answer: The Resources section is the only mandatory section — it's where you define all the AWS resources to create. Optional sections include: AWSTemplateFormatVersion (template version), Description (human-readable summary), Parameters (custom input values), Mappings (lookup tables like region-to-AMI), Outputs (values to display after creation), and Metadata.

questions.question: What is the SSM Agent and which AMIs have it pre-installed?
questions.answer: The SSM Agent is software that runs on EC2 instances (and on-premises servers) and acts as a messenger between the instance and AWS Systems Manager. It enables all SSM features — Session Manager, Run Command, Patch Manager, Inventory, and Parameter Store access. It comes pre-installed on Amazon Linux 2, Amazon Linux 2023, Amazon ECS-optimized AMIs, and Windows Server AMIs provided by AWS. Third-party and community AMIs may not have it.

questions.question: How does Session Manager work and what are its advantages over SSH?
questions.answer: Session Manager provides a browser-based or CLI shell connection to EC2 instances through the AWS Systems Manager service. It works by communicating with the SSM Agent running on the instance over AWS's internal network. Advantages over SSH: (1) No SSH keys needed — access is controlled by IAM, (2) No need to open port 22 in security groups, (3) Works with instances that have no public IP address, (4) No bastion host required, (5) All sessions can be logged to S3 or CloudWatch for auditing, (6) Revoking access is as simple as disabling an IAM user.

questions.question: What is Parameter Store and when would you use SecureString type?
questions.answer: Parameter Store is an AWS Systems Manager feature that provides secure, hierarchical storage for configuration data and secrets. It has three types: String (plain text), StringList (comma-separated values), and SecureString (KMS-encrypted). You use SecureString for any sensitive data — database passwords, API keys, tokens, connection strings. The application retrieves the value at runtime via the AWS SDK using its IAM role, so the secret is never hardcoded in code or stored in version control.

questions.question: What is the difference between Terraform and CloudFormation?
questions.answer: CloudFormation is AWS's native IaC tool — it's free, deeply integrated with AWS, and uses YAML or JSON. It only works with AWS. Terraform by HashiCorp is multi-cloud — it works with AWS, Azure, GCP, and 1000+ other providers using HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language). Terraform maintains a state file to track deployed resources; CloudFormation's state is managed by AWS internally. For AWS-only environments, either works. For multi-cloud, Terraform is the standard.

questions.question: What is Ansible and how does it differ from CloudFormation?
questions.answer: Ansible is an agentless, push-based configuration management tool. It manages software INSIDE servers — installing packages, updating config files, managing services. CloudFormation creates and manages infrastructure — the servers, networks, databases, and storage themselves. They complement each other: use CloudFormation or Terraform to create EC2 instances, then use Ansible to configure the software running on those instances. Ansible uses SSH to push tasks from a control node to target servers; target servers need no Ansible agent installed.

questions.question: What IAM permission does an EC2 instance need for AWS Systems Manager to manage it?
questions.answer: The EC2 instance needs an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy attached. This is the minimum policy required — it grants the SSM Agent permission to communicate with Systems Manager, receive commands, and report status. Using the more permissive AmazonSSMFullAccess is not recommended because it violates the principle of least privilege. The role must be attached to the EC2 instance (not to a user).

questions.question: Walk me through a situation where IaC saved your team from a major incident.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our team's AWS development environment was accidentally deleted by a misconfigured IAM policy, losing all EC2 instances, VPC configurations, security groups, and database connections that we had spent two weeks setting up manually. (Task) I needed to rebuild the entire environment within the day so development could resume. (Action) Because we had written CloudFormation templates for our infrastructure, I ran 'aws cloudformation create-stack' with our template, specifying the correct parameters for the dev environment. (Result) The complete environment was recreated in 15 minutes — identical to what we had before. After this incident, the team adopted IaC as mandatory for all environments.

questions.question: Your production application works perfectly but staging keeps failing. How would you investigate and fix this?
questions.answer: (Situation) The staging environment was set up differently from production — manually by a different engineer — so configurations drifted over time. (Task) Identify the discrepancy and ensure both environments are identical going forward. (Action) First, I used AWS Systems Manager Inventory to collect a full software and configuration snapshot of both environments. I compared the installed packages, environment variables, and config files. After finding the difference (a missing environment variable and a different nginx version), I fixed staging. Then I wrote a CloudFormation template for both environments and Ansible playbooks for configuration, ensuring future environments are built from identical code. (Result) Staging and production matched. No further environment drift issues.

questions.question: A security audit requires that all EC2 access be logged and no SSH keys be used. How do you implement this?
questions.answer: (Situation) The auditors flagged SSH key usage as a security risk and required full audit trails of all server access. (Task) Eliminate SSH keys and implement auditable access for 30 EC2 instances. (Action) I: (1) Removed all SSH inbound rules from all security groups, (2) Removed key pair associations where possible, (3) Created IAM roles for all team members with Session Manager permissions, (4) Attached AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore roles to all EC2 instances, (5) Enabled Session Manager logging — all sessions now stream to an S3 bucket with CloudTrail enabled. (Result) Zero SSH keys in use. Every session is logged with the IAM user identity, commands run, and timestamps. Audit requirement satisfied.

questions.question: How would you roll out a critical security patch to 200 EC2 instances with minimal disruption?
questions.answer: (Situation) A critical CVE was released requiring an immediate nginx security update. (Task) Apply the patch to 200 production EC2 instances without taking down the application. (Action) (1) Used SSM Patch Manager in Scan mode to identify which instances were vulnerable, (2) Applied the patch first to development instances via Run Command, tested the application, (3) Used Patch Manager with a maintenance window to roll out to staging, verified, (4) Used Patch Manager with a separate maintenance window for production — applied in waves of 25 at a time to avoid taking everything down simultaneously, (5) Monitored patch compliance dashboard for results. (Result) All 200 instances patched within 2 hours. Zero application downtime. Full compliance report generated automatically.

questions.question: How would you securely pass a database password to an application running on EC2?
questions.answer: (Situation) Our application needs the production RDS password but storing it in code or environment variables is a security risk. (Task) Provide the password securely without hardcoding it. (Action) (1) Stored the password in Parameter Store as a SecureString under /myapp/prod/db-password with KMS encryption, (2) Created an IAM policy allowing only that specific parameter path to be read, (3) Attached a role with this policy to the EC2 instance, (4) Updated the application code to call the SSM GetParameter API at startup to retrieve the password. (Result) The password never appears in code, environment variables, or logs. Rotating the password only requires updating the Parameter Store value — no code changes needed.

questions.question: Describe the CloudFormation stack lifecycle from creation to deletion.
questions.answer: (Situation) A developer asks how CloudFormation manages the full lifecycle of a stack. (Task) Explain each phase. (Action) The lifecycle has four phases: (1) CREATE — CloudFormation reads the template, validates it, and provisions all resources in dependency order. If any resource fails, it auto-rolls back. (2) UPDATE — You submit a new template version. Best practice: create a Change Set first to preview what will change. CloudFormation updates resources in-place or replaces them as needed. (3) DRIFT DETECTION — CloudFormation can detect if resources were manually changed outside of CloudFormation. (4) DELETE — CloudFormation deletes all resources in the stack in reverse dependency order. Deletion fails if resources have manual protection or are referenced by other stacks. (Result) The stack is managed as a single unit throughout its entire lifecycle.

questions.question: What is your recommendation when a team is debating between CloudFormation and Terraform?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team is starting a new project and evaluating IaC tools. (Task) Provide a structured recommendation. (Action) I'd ask three questions: (1) Are you AWS-only or multi-cloud? CloudFormation is excellent for AWS-only environments and offers deep native integration. Terraform is better for multi-cloud. (2) Does your team have existing Terraform experience? Adoption cost matters. (3) Do you need state file management? CloudFormation manages state for you; Terraform requires a remote backend (S3 + DynamoDB) for team use. My recommendation: For AWS-only with no multi-cloud plans, CloudFormation is simpler and free. For multi-cloud or existing HashiCorp tooling, Terraform. (Result) The team can make an informed decision based on their specific requirements rather than hype.

questions.question: How would you design a CloudFormation template that deploys differently based on the environment (dev/prod)?
questions.answer: (Situation) Same application, different configurations for dev and prod — different instance types, different retention periods, different scaling. (Task) Build a single reusable template. (Action) Use three techniques together: (1) Parameters — accept an 'Environment' parameter (dev/prod). (2) Conditions — define conditions like IsProduction: !Equals [!Ref Environment, prod], then use Condition: IsProduction on resources to conditionally create prod-only resources. (3) Mappings — map environment to config values (e.g., dev instance type = t3.micro, prod = t3.large). Use !FindInMap to retrieve the correct value. (Result) One template, two deployments, correctly configured for each environment — no duplicate code, no manual changes between environments.

questions.question: Why is Ansible called agentless? How does this compare to Chef and Puppet?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team is evaluating configuration management tools. (Task) Explain the architectural difference. (Action) Ansible is agentless because target servers need zero special software installed. Ansible uses SSH to push tasks from the control node (master) to targets. This makes setup simple — any server accessible via SSH can be managed immediately. Chef and Puppet require an agent installed on every target server. These agents run continuously and pull configuration from the Chef/Puppet master server at regular intervals (pull model). This means: Ansible — simpler setup, push model, SSH required. Chef/Puppet — more powerful scheduling, pull model, agents required, more complex setup. (Result) For most use cases, Ansible's agentless approach is simpler. Chef/Puppet are better when you need guaranteed configuration convergence on a strict schedule without manual triggers.

questions.question: What is Terraform state and what problems arise without proper remote state management?
questions.answer: Terraform's state file (terraform.tfstate) is its record of what infrastructure currently exists. When you run 'terraform plan', Terraform compares your .tf files (desired state) against the state file (current state) to determine what to create, change, or destroy. Without remote state management: (1) If each developer has a local state file, they'll have conflicting views of reality — one developer might try to create a resource that another already created. (2) State files can be corrupted if two people run 'terraform apply' simultaneously. (3) Local state files get lost if a developer's laptop is lost. Solution: Store state in an S3 bucket (shared, durable) with DynamoDB for state locking (prevents concurrent applies). This is the production standard for team Terraform usage.

questions.question: How do CloudFormation Nested Stacks work and when would you use them?
questions.answer: Nested Stacks let you reference one CloudFormation stack from inside another using the AWS::CloudFormation::Stack resource type. The parent stack creates and manages child stacks. Use nested stacks when: (1) A single template approaches the 500-resource limit, (2) You want to reuse common infrastructure components (a VPC template reused by multiple application stacks), (3) Teams own separate pieces of infrastructure that need to be composed together. The parent stack passes parameters to nested stacks and can reference their Outputs. This is the CloudFormation equivalent of modular programming — breaking a large system into manageable, reusable components.

questions.question: What is CloudFormation drift detection and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Drift occurs when someone manually changes an AWS resource that was created by CloudFormation — for example, changing a security group rule directly in the console instead of updating the template. CloudFormation Drift Detection compares the current actual state of resources against the last known template configuration and identifies any differences. It matters because: (1) Drifted resources can cause template update failures, (2) Manual changes break the 'single source of truth' principle of IaC, (3) In regulated industries, drift is a compliance violation. Best practice: prohibit manual changes to CloudFormation-managed resources, use IAM policies to enforce this, and run drift detection regularly as part of compliance checks.

questions.question: Describe a highly available, multi-region architecture you would deploy using IaC. What challenges does multi-region IaC introduce?
questions.answer: For a highly available architecture, I would use: Primary region (us-east-1) — EC2 in an Auto Scaling Group behind an ALB, RDS Multi-AZ, S3 with cross-region replication enabled. Secondary region (ap-south-1) — identical stack using the same CloudFormation template with region-specific parameter values, RDS read replica promoted to primary during failover, Route 53 health-check-based failover routing. Multi-region IaC challenges: (1) AMI IDs differ per region — solved with Mappings or SSM Parameter Store dynamic references, (2) Deploying to multiple regions requires running the stack in each region separately or using StackSets, (3) Global resources like IAM roles and Route 53 exist once — handled in a separate global stack, (4) State management in Terraform needs region-specific state files. Solution: Use CloudFormation StackSets for automated multi-region deployment, or Terraform workspaces.

questions.question: How would you implement a zero-downtime blue-green deployment using CloudFormation?
questions.answer: Blue-green deployment runs two identical production environments simultaneously, switching traffic from the current (blue) to the new (green). IaC implementation: (1) The CloudFormation template creates an Auto Scaling Group + Launch Template + ALB Target Group. (2) For a new deployment, create a second (green) stack with the new AMI/config — it creates new EC2 instances behind a new target group. (3) Use an ALB with weighted target group routing — initially 100% blue, gradually shift: 90/10, then 50/50, then 100% green. (4) Monitor CloudWatch metrics during traffic shift. (5) If green looks healthy, set to 100% and delete the blue stack. (6) If issues arise, shift back to 100% blue instantly. CloudFormation manages the entire lifecycle of each environment as a named stack.

questions.question: How does SSM Parameter Store differ from AWS Secrets Manager, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: Both store secrets securely, but they have key differences: Parameter Store is part of Systems Manager — free for Standard parameters (up to 10,000), with optional KMS encryption (SecureString). It does NOT auto-rotate secrets. Secrets Manager is a dedicated secrets service — has a cost (~$0.40/secret/month), always encrypts with KMS, and supports automatic secret rotation (e.g., auto-rotate RDS password every 30 days). Use Parameter Store for: application configuration values, non-rotating secrets, cost-sensitive scenarios, config values you reference alongside actual secrets. Use Secrets Manager for: database credentials that must auto-rotate, third-party API keys with rotation support, scenarios where rotation SLAs are a compliance requirement. In practice, many teams use Parameter Store for config and non-rotating secrets, and Secrets Manager only when rotation is required.
